bull.b: Revenue growth from ~$31.6B in 2022 to ~$45.2B in 2025 and ~$48.4B TTM, alongside net-margin expansion to ~29% TTM, indicates that scale is translating into stronger earnings power. This supports sustained investment in content and product initiatives while improving resilience across cycles.

Operating cash flow reached ~$11.8B and free cash flow ~$11.0B TTM, with FCF conversion of net income around 0.93–0.95 in 2023–TTM. Reliable internal cash generation gives Netflix greater capacity to fund content, repay or refinance obligations, and return capital without relying solely on external financing.

Netflix has approximately 330 million subscription households, yet household penetration remains below 45% of an estimated 800 million addressable households. This combination of global scale and remaining reach provides a durable platform for membership growth, pricing, advertising, and newer interactive offerings over the coming years.

bear.b: Absolute debt remains meaningful at roughly $14–18 billion despite debt-to-equity improving to about 0.54x. The refinancing of near-term maturities helps timing, but ongoing obligations can still constrain financial flexibility and increase exposure if operating performance or cash generation weakens.

First-half 2026 view hours increased only 2%, or about 1.5 billion hours, reflecting softness in raw viewing hours per member. If engagement does not keep pace with membership growth, Netflix may face greater pressure to sustain retention, justify pricing, and convert its large audience into higher monetization.

Planned 2026 content expense growth of roughly 10% exceeds the five-year average of about 8%. While investment can support the slate, faster spending growth raises the execution burden: revenue, engagement, and margins must continue improving enough to preserve cash conversion and profitability.
